property_summary: If receiver != address(0) and amount > 0 then calling c.sendTo(receiver, amount) (when invoked from this test contract) does not revert.

For any caller/receiver/amount, calling sendTo on the correct contract never reverts solely due to attempting to transfer more than the contract balance (the transfer may revert but the function call semantics allow trying any amount), whereas the mutant proactively prevents attempts to transfer amounts greater than address(this).balance by reverting earlier; thus there exist inputs where the mutant rejects a call that the reference would accept (i.e., the reference will attempt the transfer call while the mutant pre-checks and reverts).

For any caller/receiver/amount where the contract has at least `amount` wei balance, sendTo succeeds (does not revert) on the reference C; the mutant adds a pre-check reverting when amount > address(this).balance, so there exist inputs (amount > current balance) where the mutant reverts but the reference would proceed (and may later revert or succeed depending on the receiver), violating this universal success property.

For any caller, receiver contract, and amount, the reference C will attempt the transfer when sendTo is called (so the call does not preemptively reject based on c's balance); the mutant adds a precondition requiring amount <= address(this).balance, causing some inputs (amount > c.balance) to revert immediately while the reference would still attempt the transfer, so the mutant breaks this universal attempt-to-transfer property.

For any caller, receiver contract and amount, if the receiver's fallback/receive REVERTS then the reference C will itself revert (because transfer bubbles revert) for any positive amount, whereas the mutant that pre-checks amount <= address(this).balance will accept (not revert) some calls the reference would revert when amount exceeds balance — therefore the universal rule: for any receiver that always reverts, calling sendTo(reveter, amount) should always revert on the reference; the mutant can make some of these calls succeed (not revert) by preemptively blocking transfers when amount > balance — we assert that for a always-reverting receiver the reference always causes the call to revert.

For any sender who is owner, any non-zero amount and any non-zero receiver address, if the receiver's fallback always reverts then calling sendTo(...) on the correct contract always reverts (because transfer bubbles), but the mutant can pre-check c.balance and therefore may NOT attempt the transfer and thus may NOT revert for some inputs (amount > c.balance), violating the universal 'always-reverts' rule.
Calling sendTo must never leave address(c).balance decreased while address(this).balance unchanged when amount == 0 (i.e., zero-value transfer should not change balances).
When amount is zero, sendTo must revert (so reverted == true for amount == 0).

For any caller who is the contract owner and any non-zero receiver/address and positive amount, calling sendTo will either revert on failure (so a failing transfer causes the call to revert) — the reference using transfer always reverts on failure, while the mutant using send may silently succeed (not revert) when the low-level payment fails.

For any nonzero amount and nonzero receiver, sendTo always either forwards funds and reduces contract balance (in reference it reverts on failure so the contract balance never decreases unless transfer succeeded); the mutant that uses unchecked call can leave the contract balance unchanged when the external transfer fails without reverting — thus the invariant that address(c).balance decreases by amount when sendTo returns successfully is broken by the mutant for failing callee cases.

For any nonzero amount sent by the owner to a nonzero receiver, C.sendTo either reverts (on failure) or succeeds and reduces address(c).balance by exactly amount; the mutant which ignores call return can succeed (not revert) while leaving c's balance unchanged when the callee reverts, violating this balance-change property.
